hook: Noland Arbaugh became the first person to receive Neuralink's N1 brain implant, in January 2024, eight years after a swimming accident left him paralyzed below the shoulders. With the device he moves a computer cursor by imagining movement, which let him play chess, handle email and play video games without help. His public account of losing much of that control when most of the implant's threads retracted, and of regaining it after Neuralink changed its software, made his case a widely reported test of how an early brain-computer interface holds up in daily use.

quick_facts: Received Neuralink's N1 implant in January 2024 as the first participant in the company's human trial. He was the first Neuralink recipient, not the first person with an implanted brain-computer interface.
Grew up in Yuma, Arizona, and studied international studies at Texas A&M University, where he was a member of the Corps of Cadets.
Has been paralyzed below the shoulders since a swimming accident in June 2016, while working as a summer camp counselor in Pennsylvania.
The N1 implant carries 64 threads with 1,024 electrodes. About a month after his surgery, Neuralink found that 85 percent of his threads had retracted, and it disclosed the problem in May 2024.
Texas A&M reported in June 2024 that he was spending more than 40 hours a week helping Neuralink engineers test the device.
By August 2025, Fortune reported, he was using the implant about 10 hours a day, taking community college prerequisites toward a neuroscience degree and building a paid public speaking business.
